sections.text:
“For whom is woe? For whom sorrow? For whom distress and darkness? For whom eternal condemnation?” Is it not for transgressors? Is it not for those who have denied the faith? And what demonstrates their denial? Is it not that they have set aside their own confessions?

What did they confess, and when? They confessed faith in the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit when, renouncing the devil and his angels, they uttered that saving confession.

What appropriate name, then, have the children of light for such people? Are they not called transgressors because they have violated the covenants of their salvation? What shall I call one who denies God? What shall I call one who denies Christ? What else but a transgressor? And what name would you have me give to one who denies the Spirit? Must it not be the same, since that person has violated the covenant made with God?

If confession of faith in the Spirit brings the blessedness of true religion, while denial subjects a person to condemnation for godlessness, how dreadful it is to reject that confession now—not through fear of fire, sword, cross, scourges, wheels, or instruments of torture, but merely through the sophistries and deceptions of those who fight against the Spirit.

I testify to every person who confesses Christ while denying God that Christ will profit such a person nothing; and to the one who calls upon God while rejecting the Son, that the faith is empty; and to the one who sets aside the Spirit, that faith in the Father and Son will become fruitless—for one cannot truly possess that faith without the Spirit being present.

For the one who does not believe in the Spirit does not believe in the Son, and the one who has not believed in the Son does not believe in the Father. “No one can say, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except in the Holy Spirit”; and, “No one has ever seen God; the only-begotten God who is in the bosom of the Father has made him known.”

Such a person has no share in true worship, for it is impossible to worship the Son except in the Holy Spirit, and impossible to call upon the Father except in the Spirit of adoption.

translator_notes: Direct Mercy translation from Basil's Greek PG 32 text.
The chapter connects denial of the Spirit with violation of the baptismal confession.
The polemical language is retained as Basil's fourth-century theological argument.
